profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for a follow-up ML research project inspired by a recent review on deep reinforcement learning for machine scheduling. The lab wants to turn the review into a concrete reproducibility benchmark and short workshop paper comparing representative DRL scheduler families on classic job-shop scheduling instances before extending to dynamic variants. The agenda is to set the initial experiment scope, decide what the first milestone should include, divide responsibilities between methodology framing and implementation, and align on the end-of-month internal deadline ahead of a workshop submission six weeks later. The expected outcome is a shared plan for what the 'pilot' consists of, what 'coverage' from the review means operationally, which benchmark instances to start from, and what must exist by the internal release date.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: Deep reinforcement learning, empirical ML methodology, benchmarking studies
members.background: Leads a university ML systems lab and recently co-authored a survey on DRL for combinatorial optimization, with a focus on turning broad literature into concise comparative studies.
members.private_state: She wants a fast, credible benchmark package that is sufficient to support a workshop paper and establish the lab's position on reproducibility gaps, while avoiding a long infrastructure build that would delay submission.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'pilot results,' it means just enough runs to reveal whether the benchmark setup is behaving sensibly and which architecture families are worth keeping for the paper.

When they say they will 'mirror the review's coverage,' that mainly refers to representing the major DRL architecture families discussed in the review, not recreating every non-DRL comparator from the original papers.
References to 'FT10 and LA instances' naturally mean the standard OR-Library job-shop benchmarks as already wrapped in the group's JobShopLib-based codebase.
An 'internal release' is complete once one lab member can run the main pipeline end-to-end on the cluster from the documented configuration, even if packaging and cleanup are still rough.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Manufacturing simulation, reproducible ML infrastructure, scheduling environments
members.background: Previously built digital-twin simulators for factory scheduling and now maintains the lab's experiment harnesses, with a strong bias toward reusable artifacts and stable evaluation pipelines.
members.private_state: He wants to use this project to create a durable benchmark stack the lab can reuse for future papers, and he is concerned that a loosely defined milestone will create rework if the code is not reproducible from the start.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' should already be table-ready on a small benchmark slice, including seed sweeps and scripts that regenerate the exact summary values the group will discuss.

If the team says they will reproduce the review's 'coverage,' that includes the classical heuristics and OR baselines that the reviewed DRL papers were compared against, because otherwise the benchmark is not context-complete.

Mentions of 'FT10 and LA' refer to the lab's simulator versions of those instances, which already apply the house preprocessing conventions such as normalized processing times and the standard wrapper format.

An 'internal release' means a fresh clone by another lab member should reproduce the pilot tables locally or on the cluster without manual intervention, with environment files, run scripts, and fixed seeds included.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need 'pilot results' before scaling up.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a lightweight sanity-check package: a few representative runs on initial instances, enough to see whether the setup works and whether the architectural categories produce sensible relative behavior.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a mini-final benchmark: a small but publication-shaped subset with multi-seed runs, stable aggregation scripts, and tables that can be directly circulated to the group.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research planning, 'pilot results' is a familiar and cooperative phrase that sounds precise enough; both think they are endorsing an obvious early milestone, so neither feels a need to operationalize it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'mirror the review's coverage' in the initial benchmark.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the scope is limited to representative DRL model families from the review—such as conventional policy networks, encoder-decoder models, and graph-based approaches—because the purpose is to compare DRL design patterns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the scope also includes the standard non-DRL comparators used in the reviewed papers—dispatching heuristics and OR baselines—because without them the reproduced benchmark lacks the comparison frame the literature uses.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'coverage from the review' feels like a natural shorthand for prior shared reading, and both participants believe the missing details are already implied by the paper's structure.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'FT10 and LA instances' they are starting from
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to begin with 'FT10 and LA instances' for the first milestone.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the canonical OR-Library instances as accessed through the group's existing JobShopLib wrapper, with standard raw processing times and the lab's default evaluation parser.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the lab-maintained simulator versions labeled FT10 and LA, which preserve the same instance names but pass through the internal preprocessing pipeline and wrapper conventions he usually uses.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The benchmark names are standard and widely recognized, so their shared shorthand creates false confidence that they mean the exact same instantiated files and wrappers.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'internal release by end of month' requires
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree there should be an 'internal release' by the end of the month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the release is successful if the main experiment path is runnable for internal discussion, with enough documentation for the group to inspect outputs and continue iterating.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the release is successful only if another lab member can reproduce the pilot tables from a fresh checkout using packaged environments, fixed seeds, and scripted execution.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use internal deadlines as soft checkpoints, so the same milestone label sounds aligned even though they apply different completion standards to it.

turns.inner_thought: I need this framed as a reproducibility benchmark, but the real constraint is time. If we can get a credible first package running by the end of the month, that gives me enough to anchor a workshop submission and make the reproducibility-gap argument without sinking us into a giant infrastructure effort. For me, an internal release just means the main path works on the cluster and the group can inspect outputs and iterate from there.

To do that, we need a clear first milestone and an internal release by the end of the month so we're not still debating setup details in week five.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a deadline helps, but only if the milestone is solid. Starting from FT10 and a few LA instances makes sense, and in my head that's the simulator versions we already keep under the lab harness with the usual preprocessing, because that gets us onto reusable rails immediately.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I think the cleanest way to start is pilot results on FT10 and a few LA instances, then build outward from there. If we set it up that way, the harness is useful right away instead of becoming a one-off.

And when I say mirror the review's coverage, I mean representative DRL architecture families from the survey, not every comparator from the original scheduling papers.

turns.inner_thought: So he owns the pilot and gets us something the group can run and inspect; I can use that to shape the workshop story around benchmark categories from the review and reproducibility gaps.
